title: The Freedom of the Savior in Hades
english: so that from this there might come rest

He was excessively liberated, from the more excellent staying and guarding in Hades—not according to punishments, but regarding the guarding... being hidden there, 'until the wrath passes' (Rom 13:10), as it is being said of God to remember him, in order to say more clearly that he would rather receive the time of his resurrection in Hades than undergo so many pains.

For indeed, he who truly experiences in Hades according to each one, the righteous man lives better during the time before the coming of Christ, since he is about to be liberated from the clamorous and sickly body to enjoy the incorruptible. For the Savior, according to the human, was not subject to being in Hades, even if it happened there through others. For it has been said of himself: 'I became as a helpless man among the dead, yet free' (Acts 2:24). And indeed, angels lead the holy ones, but the wicked ones, the shadows. But the Savior, being free, did not need angels, being master of them and being ministered to and led by them. For he said: 'No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down myself' (John 10:18).

But also in the Song of Songs, through symbols, he says he is smelling the myrrh of death, showing himself free: 'I will go my own way to the mountain of myrrh' (Song 1:4). And also 'there is no man of the nations with me' (Song 1:5) shows his unattached state according to the human. Instead of this, another interprets 'I alone shall drink the wine-cup.' But also, when Peter says: 'I will lay down my soul for you,' he rebukes him, saying: 'You will lay down your soul for me? Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times' (Matt 26:34).

Because the holy ones are led by light-bringing angels and the wicked ones by dark demons, it has been said: 'O fool, in this night take your soul from you,' implying they are punished. And concerning Lazarus it is said: 'It happened when the poor man died, he was carried by the angels to Abraham's bosom' (Luke 16:22), clearly by good angels. For if a man dies, he will live having completed the days of his life. Not unsuitably, being persuaded and knowing concerning the resurrection of the dead, he places the more excellent deliverance from the painful life here, that it is more beautiful 'to be dissolved and to be with Christ' (Phil 1:23), saying: 'for if...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Resurrection as a New Birth
english: "If a man dies, he shall live having completed the days of his life" (Job 14:14), from which a doctrine concerning resurrection is presented and a judgment of each life in this life, not occurring randomly or by chance when death happens. And even if "having completed the days of his life" can signify the days before the resurrection, consider also that which the eternal life shall receive: "I will wait, until I become again."

In the same sequence of words, and the opinions of those previously arguing against him, are placed alongside the true ones, so that while they lie parallel, we may see which are being dismantled and which are being constructed. For he was saying, regarding their erroneous opinion: "but a man having fallen asleep shall not rise" and "a man having ended his life has gone, and a fallen mortal is no longer." For the nature of man did not have it as they thought, that having possessed subsistence until the present life, having cast off this life, he is no longer, just like the irrational animals.

For the souls of irrational animals are scattered with their bodies, and therefore they are destroyed. But since the [nature] of man is not scattered, nor is he destroyed; for he is immortal. And since the friends did not depart, as it happens through painful struggle just as it happened to him the blessed one, considering that he suffers because of sin, opposing their opinion, he says the calculation that to bear the painful things is to become again. "I will wait," for he says, "until I become again," signifying the resurrection, which those saying [he is] being destroyed do not accept, [some] placing the nature of [the soul]... but the "I will wait, until I become again" [is part] of "if a man dies, he shall live having completed the days of his life."

Possessing this presupposition, the blessed Paul also wrote: "if in this life we hope only, we are more to be pitied than all men" (1 Cor 15:19) and "if I have fought as a wild beast against men in Ephesus, what is my profit, if the dead are not raised?" (1 Cor 15:32) Thus, not setting aside the opinion of the friends, that it is through virtue to suffer, the [saying] "but a man having fallen asleep shall not rise" was said...

But 'I will respond to you when you call again' stands in opposition to the opinion of those who mock: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isa 22:13). The phrase 'until I become again' must be explained in this way: resurrection is a kind of birth. For this reason, 're-birth' is spoken in relation to the Savior. For the former birth, having a different manner, consisted by the change of matter, either as dust in the first maker, or as the side as in the Eve of the seeds as in those born, or by a virgin turning something of herself into the salvific womb, such being the change. Thus also of the resurrection, whether it is a transfer into the dust of the body, or into something else according to these changes, the rising body is raised incorruptible. It is, therefore, a birth.

Then 'you will call, and I will respond to you.' Wishing to show that not only the body is raised, but also the soul possessing the thoughts concerning God, he says, 'you will call, and I will respond to you.' For to listen to God calling is proper to a rational being. 'Do not cast away the works of your hands' (Ps 31:5). Having taught concerning the resurrection of the whole human and the immortality of the soul, he instructs his friends so as not to consider him judged as insignificant by God. 'You have enumerated my faults to me, and you will not pass over any of my sins' (Ps 32:5). Teaching an unerasable knowledge of him, through these things he also in a certain way instructs his friends who are at odds, that through sin he suffers, how he must repent and not be arrogant regarding the purity existing within him, for the sake of moderation toward himself and toward them, raising them to repentance by saying these things. 'I will note if I have passed by unintentionally' (Ps 51:6). As if speaking to them again, he says these things while they are at odds, as if he were undergoing these things as a sinner, and by moderation and for their instruction, so that they might imitate him being so pure and bringing forth words of repentance. 'You have sealed my iniquities in a bag' (Ps 51:6). That is to say: 'You have included in them both the quality and the number.' And it is necessary to perceive these things also, similar to the former. And besides, a falling mountain will fall. Believing in the cause of all things, that he will complete the contest.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Rejection and the Sinner's Delusion
english: Having crushed the one who requested the mountain called here, he says to them that 'he will weaken so as to fall from the expectation which he expected, trying to see me.' For indeed all request, as it is foretold, but they do not know that the purpose of the opponent will fall away. And the rock will be made old from its place. Even if the opponent thinks himself to be the rock, 'it will be made old'—instead of 'a stumbling block shall be seen'—signifying the appearance of correctness.

And the rock is mentioned because it sends out the impression as unshakeable, and because Christ is being formed and is an imitator of the true rock, concerning which it was said: 'And the rock was Christ' (1 Cor 10:4). And he calls the state here a place, according to which the virtuous man wishes to see. Since the place is also called a step, it is said in the Acts: 'Master, Knower of hearts, reveal one to take the place of this ministry from which Judas passed' (Acts 1:20).

And even after saying that 'you sealed my iniquities in a bag' (Ps 69:6) and how regarding his own sin he had brought forward the previously set forth things, he applied 'but the mountain falling shall fall, and the rock shall be made old from its place' (Job 14:10) to show that 'even if a mountain arises through pride or through hardness, its condemnation shall be,' having perceived this. Waters smoothed the stones, and waters overwhelmed the depths of the earth's soil; and did you destroy the endurance of man? He confirms through these things the previously spoken, that repentance is powerful.

For through 'waters smoothed the stones' (Job 14:11), he demonstrates that the one beginning to repent, persisting in this, according to the water which removes the excess from the stone, frees himself from the superfluities of sin, as if no longer having the roughness from it, and just as lying in the depths of soils, he works the flood of sin. 'If these things have this manner, do not recognize the endurance of man, nor say that this is destroyed when it has worn him down and gone to an end.' He moves the word toward God. For after saying that repentance is possible and that one must not lose hope in man, he brings the 'having worn him down and gone to an end' as an instruction, that unless God is a co-worker, the things of endurance are in vain. 'If...

For unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it (Ps 127:1). God does not push away the worthy person, but the one positioned in such a way, saying: 'Depart from me, workers of iniquity, I never knew you' (Matt 7:23). He turns His face away and drives them out.

It is said: 'The face of the Lord is against those doing evil' (Ps 2:5); and again the saints pray: 'Let your face shine and we shall be saved' (Ps 67:1); and in others: 'May His face shine upon you and give you peace' (Num 6:25). Therefore, if the sinner, through God's great patience, remains unfeeling toward his failings, not thinking himself to be God, but desiring to remain hidden, saying: 'Darkness covers me from every side and the walls, who sees me?', God says: 'I am a God drawing near and not a God far off. Shall anyone hide in secret and I shall not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord' (Jer 23:24).

Having turned His face from the sinner, He sends him away, instead of 'showing him to be a stranger to Himself,' according to: 'God will drive them away because they did not listen to Him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Deut 32:28) and: 'Like wounded women cast down sleeping in a grave, of whom you no longer remembered, and they themselves were driven from your hand' (Isa 57:1). And though many of His sons became [so], he did not know; even if a few became [so], he does not know.

Understand, lest these things reveal the ungraspable nature of God's judgments. Rather, his flesh grieved and his soul mourned. This shows that as the wrath against the sinner moves according to the secret words of providence, the one falling into it suffers and mourns, but is ignorant of the words of the handing over. These things are instructional, so as not to say to friends that they know that one suffers through sin.

For the one who does not endure suffers and is consumed when he falls into calamities, but the brave man, even if he is stung by hardships, bears them courageously toward the goal, looking away (Heb 12:2). For only the one who seeks nothing good or useful suffers if he is afflicted. But the virtuous man, like a crowned athlete, does not regard the hardships because of the expectation of the crown. Having understood, Eliphaz the Temanite says: Whether the wise man will give an answer of the understanding of the spirit? And this one of the same...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
